questions.q: What are tides, and how are spring and neap tides caused?

answer.text: Tides are the regular rise and fall of the level of ocean water, occurring usually twice a day. They are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon, and to a lesser extent of the Sun, together with the effect of the Earth's rotation.

When the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a straight line, at the time of the new moon and the full moon, the pulls of the Sun and the Moon act together. This produces the highest high tides and lowest low tides, called spring tides.

When the Sun and Moon are at right angles to the Earth, at the first and last quarters of the Moon, their pulls partly cancel each other. This gives tides of smaller range, called neap tides, with lower high tides and higher low tides.

answer: Tides are important for navigation, fishing and generating tidal power.

questions.q: How do ocean currents influence the climate and economic activities of coastal regions?
answer: Ocean currents, the large-scale movements of surface water, have a strong influence on coastal climates and human activity.

answer.text: Warm currents raise the temperature of the coasts they wash, keeping ports ice-free and climates milder, as the Gulf Stream does for north-west Europe. Cold currents lower coastal temperatures and reduce rainfall; where they flow along the western coasts of continents they help form deserts such as the Atacama and the Namib.

Where warm and cold currents meet, as at the Grand Banks off Newfoundland, the mixing of waters brings up nutrients and creates some of the world's richest fishing grounds, though it also produces dense fog.
Sailors have long used currents to speed their voyages.

answer: Thus currents shape both the weather and the livelihoods of coastal peoples.
